slides.title: Secure by Design, Not Secure by Patch
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: CISA's April 2023 'Secure by Design' pledge was co-signed by Microsoft, Google, and AWS. NIST SP 800-218 (SSDF) organizes practices into Prepare the Organization, Protect the Software, Produce Well-Secured Software, and Respond to Vulnerabilities.

Misconception: Students think a web application firewall in front of vulnerable code is 'good enough' security. It is a deadbolt on a house with unlocked windows, the professor's note analogy from the ebook.

Analogy: Building a house and only thinking about locks after the walls and windows are installed, you can bolt on a deadbolt, but you never audited the windows.

Exam tip: If asked to contrast 'secure by design' with a WAF or perimeter-only approach, name the trade-off: perimeter controls catch exploitation after the fact; secure design eliminates the class at construction.
bullets: Core idea: Secure Web Application Design eliminates vulnerability classes at construction time, not after deployment
The old model: 'Penetrate and patch', write functional code, test afterward, fix under deadline pressure
Cost economics: A defect caught at design costs roughly an order of magnitude less to fix than one caught in production
Two companion principles: Secure-by-design (security is a primary design constraint) and secure-by-default (safest configuration ships out of the box)
Formalized by: CISA's 2023 'Secure by Design' pledge and NIST SP 800-218 (Secure Software Development Framework)

content_blocks: Most breach post-mortems arrive at the same conclusion: the vulnerability was baked into the application during design, not introduced by a uniquely sophisticated adversary. Secure Web Application Design is the discipline of eliminating entire vulnerability classes at the point of construction rather than relying on perimeter controls like firewalls to catch exploitation after the fact.

Historically, application security was a downstream concern, developers wrote functional code, and a separate team tested it afterward under deadline pressure. This 'penetrate and patch' cycle is expensive: a defect caught during design costs roughly an order of magnitude less to fix than the same defect caught in production, echoing well-documented software defect economics.

Two companion principles operationalize secure-by-design thinking: secure-by-design means security is a primary constraint from the first architecture diagram, and secure-by-default means the out-of-the-box configuration is already the safest reasonable one, without requiring the customer to enable protections manually.

slides.title: The Web Application as a Trust Boundary
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Formal threat-modeling methods like STRIDE require explicit diagramming of every trust boundary crossing in a system.

Misconception: Students think trust boundaries are only a server-side concept. A page rendered in the user's own browser using a third-party script is still a trust boundary, foreshadow the British Airways case study.

Analogy: A customs checkpoint at a border, everything crossing from 'outside' to 'inside' must be inspected, no matter how many times it has crossed before.

Exam tip: When asked to identify the vulnerability underlying an OWASP Top 10 category, trace it back to an unmediated trust-boundary crossing.
bullets: Trust boundary: The line separating data/code a system trusts from data it must validate before use
Where it lives: Between the user's browser (untrusted) and the server's business logic/database (trusted)
Every crossing matters: A SQL query, a rendered HTML page, a filesystem path, an OS command, an authorization decision
OWASP Top 10: The industry's ranked risk taxonomy, dominated by trust-boundary failures (injection, broken access control, misconfiguration)
The discipline in one sentence: Rigorously manage what happens at every trust-boundary crossing

content_blocks: The theoretical backbone of secure-by-design thinking is recognizing that a web application is fundamentally a trust boundary problem. Every web application accepts input from an inherently untrusted source, the end user's browser, and that input eventually crosses into a trusted execution context: a SQL query, an HTML page rendered to other users, a filesystem path, an operating system command, or an authorization decision.

The entire discipline of secure coding can be summarized as rigorously managing what happens at each of these boundary crossings. The OWASP Top 10, the industry's most widely cited taxonomy of application risk, is dominated by exactly these failures: injection, broken access control, cryptographic failures, and security misconfiguration are all, at their root, cases where untrusted input or an unsafe default was allowed to influence a trusted operation without adequate mediation.

slides.title: Defense-in-Depth at the Application Layer
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: This connects directly to earlier units' network-layer defense-in-depth (firewalls, segmentation, IDS/IPS), Topic 5.5 is the application-layer mirror of that same philosophy.

Misconception: Students think 'we have a firewall' answers a question about application security. Push back: firewalls cannot see inside an HTTPS-encrypted, syntactically valid SQL query.

Analogy: A castle with a moat, walls, and guards, no single barrier is trusted alone.

Exam tip: When a scenario mentions a firewall or WAF as the only control on an injection-vulnerable app, flag that as insufficient, the fix must live in the application layer.
bullets: Definition: Multiple independent controls each address the same risk, so one control's failure doesn't cause full compromise
Application-layer layers: Input validation, output encoding, parameterized data access, secure configuration
Independence matters: A parameterized query stops SQLi even if validation is imperfect; encoding stops XSS even if data was stored maliciously
Mirrors network defense-in-depth: Same philosophy as firewalls + segmentation + IDS/IPS, but entirely within one codebase
Why it's necessary: A firewall cannot distinguish a legitimate SQL query from a malicious one, both travel over port 443 inside HTTPS

Context: This connects directly to earlier units' network-layer defense-in-depth (firewalls, segmentation, IDS/IPS), Topic 5.5 is the application-layer mirror of that same philosophy.

Misconception: Students think 'we have a firewall' answers a question about application security. Push back: firewalls cannot see inside an HTTPS-encrypted, syntactically valid SQL query.

content_blocks: A second conceptual pillar is defense-in-depth applied specifically to the application layer: input validation, output encoding, parameterized data access, and secure configuration are not redundant if implemented correctly, they are independent layers that each close a slightly different gap.

A parameterized query prevents SQL injection even if input validation is imperfect. Output encoding prevents cross-site scripting even if an attacker manages to store malicious data. Secure default configurations limit blast radius even if a control elsewhere fails. This layering mirrors the network-security concept of defense-in-depth, but operates entirely within the boundaries of a single application's codebase.

This is exactly why network controls and secure coding practices are complementary, not substitutable: a firewall cannot distinguish a legitimate SQL query from a malicious one, since both travel over an allowed port inside an encrypted session. Perimeter security stops what it can see; secure application design stops what perimeter security structurally cannot.

slides.title: The Secure Development Lifecycle and Its Gates

quiz.question: A security team runs automated static analysis against every commit to a CI/CD pipeline, flagging dangerous string concatenation before code merges. Which SDLC gate does this activity belong to?
options: Design/Threat Modeling
Implementation
Verification/Testing
Release
quiz.explanation: Option C is correct: SAST scanning is an automated verification activity that runs before code reaches production, regardless of whether it fires on every commit. Design/Threat Modeling (A) is the earlier phase where STRIDE-style diagrams are produced. Implementation (B) is where the code itself is written and peer-reviewed. Release (D) is the final sign-off gate, not the scanning activity itself.

slides.speaker_notes:
Context: STRIDE was introduced by Loren Kohnfelder and Praerit Garg at Microsoft in 1999 and remains the most widely taught threat-modeling framework.

Misconception: Students place threat modeling in Testing rather than Design, or code review in Verification rather than Implementation. Memorize the gate order precisely.

Analogy: Airport security checkpoints at different terminals, each gate catches a different class of problem, and skipping one lets risk flow downstream uninspected.

Exam tip: A common exam trap describes a code review finding and asks which phase it represents, code review is Implementation; a scan against a running staging environment (DAST) is Verification.
bullets: Requirements: Security requirements (auth strength, data classification, PCI-DSS/HIPAA obligations) captured alongside functional ones
Design/Threat Modeling: Structured methodologies like STRIDE enumerate attacks before code is written
Implementation: Secure coding standards, vetted libraries, peer code review
Verification/Testing: Automated SAST and DAST scanning plus manual penetration testing before production
Release and Response: Sign-off gate confirms remediation; post-release patch management follows a defined timeline

content_blocks: The SDLC embeds discrete security checkpoints, or gates, into each phase of development so a project cannot silently advance with unresolved security risk. Requirements capture security needs (authentication strength, data classification, regulatory obligations) alongside functional ones. Design/Threat Modeling uses structured methodologies such as STRIDE (Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information Disclosure, Denial of Service, Elevation of Privilege) to enumerate how the system could be attacked, producing data-flow diagrams before a line of code is written.

Implementation requires developers to write against secure coding standards, use vetted libraries rather than hand-rolled cryptography or query construction, and undergo peer review. Verification/Testing runs automated Static Application Security Testing (SAST, analyzes source code without running it) and Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST, probes the running app from outside) plus manual penetration testing. Release requires a final sign-off confirming critical/high findings are remediated. Response, aligned with NIST SP 800-218's 'Respond to Vulnerabilities' practice group, triages and patches newly discovered flaws on a defined timeline.

slides.title: Input Validation: Allowlisting Over Denylisting
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: OWASP's Input Validation Cheat Sheet recommends validation as close to the point of input as possible, but never as a substitute for output encoding or parameterized queries.

Misconception: Students think a thorough denylist is 'good enough' if it's long. Length doesn't fix the structural weakness, an attacker only needs one variant the list missed.

Analogy: A bouncer who only turns away people on a photo list (denylist) versus a bouncer who only admits people already on the guest list (allowlist), the guest-list bouncer never has to guess who might cause trouble.

Exam tip: Whenever a scenario describes blocking specific 'bad' keywords or characters, recognize it as a fragile denylist and recommend allowlisting instead.
bullets: Input validation: Checking data conforms to strict expectations (type, length, format, range) before it is acted on
Allowlisting (positive validation): Define the exact permitted set; reject everything else by default
Denylisting (negative validation): Define known-bad patterns; permit everything else, structurally weaker
Why allowlisting wins: Denylists require predicting every dangerous variant, including encoding tricks
Classic denylist failure: Blocking the literal string 'SELECT' while an attacker submits 'SeLeCt' or a URL-encoded variant

content_blocks: Input validation is the first line of defense at every trust boundary, checking that data received from a user or another system conforms to strict expectations before the application acts on it. The critical design decision is choosing between allowlisting and denylisting.

Allowlisting defines the exact, finite set of characters, formats, or values permitted, rejecting everything else by default. For a US ZIP code field, an allowlist might be 'exactly five digits', anything not matching is rejected outright. Denylisting instead defines known-bad patterns and permits everything else, which is structurally weaker: it requires the defender to anticipate every dangerous variation an attacker might invent, including case variation and encoding tricks.

Allowlisting is structurally superior because it defines security as the default state, while denylisting is a losing proposition given the near-infinite ways malicious payloads can be encoded or obfuscated.

slides.title: Canonicalization: Validating Before Full Decoding
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Path traversal is classified as CWE-22 and mapped to MITRE ATT&CK T1083 in post-exploitation contexts.

Misconception: Students think 'we validate the input' is sufficient without asking WHEN in the decode pipeline that validation occurs. Order matters as much as the check itself.

Analogy: A customs agent inspecting a sealed, encoded package before it's opened, rather than after, the dangerous contents are invisible until you actually decode/unwrap it.

Exam tip: If a scenario shows a filter checking for a literal dangerous substring but the payload uses percent-encoding or double-encoding to slip through, name it a canonicalization bypass and recommend decode-then-validate ordering.
bullets: Canonicalization: Converting data to a single standard representation before validating or acting on it
The bug: Validation runs BEFORE data is fully decoded, letting an alternate encoding smuggle a payload past the filter
Path traversal example: Checking for '../' before URL-decoding lets an attacker submit '%2e%2e%2f'
The decode step: '%2e%2e%2f' passes the literal-string check, then decodes to '../' afterward, filter bypassed
Correct order of operations: Fully decode and normalize input to canonical form FIRST, then validate

slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Path traversal is classified as CWE-22 and mapped to MITRE ATT&CK T1083 in post-exploitation contexts.

Misconception: Students think 'we validate the input' is sufficient without asking WHEN in the decode pipeline that validation occurs. Order matters as much as the check itself.

content_blocks: A particularly insidious failure mode is a canonicalization error, in which validation is performed on data before it has been fully decoded or normalized into its final form. If an application checks a submitted file path for the sequence '../' before URL-decoding the request, an attacker can submit '%2e%2e%2f', which passes the check because the literal string '../' is not present, but which decodes to '../' immediately afterward, reintroducing a path traversal vulnerability the filter was supposed to prevent.

The correct order of operations is: fully decode and normalize input to its canonical form first, then validate. Getting this order backward is one of the most common ways a seemingly correct filter is silently bypassed, because the validation logic and the interpretation logic are operating on two different representations of the same data.

code_block.content:
import urllib.parse

def naive_filter(raw_path):
    # VULNERABLE: checks BEFORE decoding
    if '../' in raw_path:
        return 'REJECTED'
    decoded = urllib.parse.unquote(raw_path)
    return f'ALLOWED, resolved to: {decoded}'

def fixed_filter(raw_path):
    # SECURE: decode to canonical form FIRST, then validate
    decoded = urllib.parse.unquote(raw_path)
    if '../' in decoded:
        return 'REJECTED (canonical form contains traversal)'
    return f'ALLOWED, resolved to: {decoded}'

payload = 'images/%2e%2e%2f%2e%2e%2fetc/passwd'
print('Naive filter:', naive_filter(payload))
print('Fixed filter:', fixed_filter(payload))

slides.title: Output Encoding Must Be Context-Aware
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: OWASP's XSS Prevention Cheat Sheet defines distinct encoding rules for each context because a single universal encoding scheme is not sufficient.

Misconception: Students think one 'escape everything' function handles all cases. Applying HTML-body encoding to data landing in a JavaScript context leaves it fully exploitable.

Analogy: Translating a warning label into the correct language for the country it's shipped to, using the wrong 'language' (encoding context) leaves the warning meaningless.

Exam tip: If a question describes 'sanitized' input that is still exploited, suspect a context/encoding mismatch as the root cause.
bullets: Output encoding: Transforming data immediately before writing it into a specific output context
Why context matters: The same data can be dangerous for different reasons depending on where it renders
HTML body context: Encode <, >, &, quotes as HTML entities
JavaScript string context: Escape quotes, backslashes, line terminators to prevent breaking out of a string literal
URL and attribute contexts: Percent-encode reserved characters; quote and encode attribute values

slides.speaker_notes:
Context: OWASP's XSS Prevention Cheat Sheet defines distinct encoding rules for each context because a single universal encoding scheme is not sufficient.

Misconception: Students think one 'escape everything' function handles all cases. Applying HTML-body encoding to data landing in a JavaScript context leaves it fully exploitable.

content_blocks: Output encoding is the primary defense against cross-site scripting (XSS), and it must be context-aware because the same piece of data can be dangerous for different reasons depending on where it is rendered. In the HTML body context, encode <, >, &, and quote characters as HTML entities so a user-supplied <script> tag renders as visible text rather than executing.

In a JavaScript string context, escape quotes, backslashes, and line terminators so injected data cannot break out of a quoted string literal and inject new script statements. In a URL context, percent-encode reserved characters so injected data cannot alter the structure of a query string or redirect target. In an HTML attribute context, quote all attribute values and encode quote characters, since an unquoted attribute allows injection via whitespace alone.

slides.title: XSS in Practice: Vulnerable Reflection vs. Encoded Output

quiz.question: A SAST scanner flags 'Insecure input reflection on page profile.php' because a GET parameter is echoed directly into an <h1> tag. What is the single best remediation?
options: Block the word 'script' from appearing anywhere in the URL
Apply context-aware HTML entity encoding (e.g., htmlspecialchars) to the value at the point it is written into the HTML response
Add a network firewall rule blocking requests with query parameters
Require the user to log in before viewing the page
quiz.explanation: Option B is correct: encoding the reflected value at the exact HTML output boundary neutralizes the payload regardless of its content. Option A is a fragile denylist trivially bypassed by case or encoding tricks. Option C is a network-layer control that cannot inspect or alter HTML output. Option D does not address the underlying reflection flaw at all.

slides.speaker_notes:
Context: This maps directly to the ebook's referenced Allsafe incident-response case, where a SAST alert flagged 'Insecure input reflection on page profile.php'.

Misconception: Students think fixing this requires rewriting the whole page. The fix is a single function call at the exact output boundary, htmlspecialchars(), not a redesign.

Analogy: Putting a message in quotation marks so a reader knows it's being reported, not being spoken as a command by the narrator.

Exam tip: ENT_QUOTES matters, without it, single-quote attribute-breakout attacks remain possible even after 'encoding'.
bullets: Root scenario: profile.php reflects a $_GET['username'] parameter directly into an <h1> without encoding
Attack: A crafted username value containing a <script> tag fetches document.cookie to an attacker server
Result of the flaw: Attacker JavaScript executes inside the victim's own authenticated browser session
The fix: Wrap the reflected value in htmlspecialchars() with ENT_QUOTES before echoing it
SAST connection: This exact pattern is what a scanner flags as 'Insecure input reflection on page profile.php'

slides.speaker_notes:
Context: SQL injection is CWE-89 and is the flagship example under OWASP A03:2021 Injection.

slides.speaker_notes:
Context: SQL injection is CWE-89 and is the flagship example under OWASP A03:2021 Injection.

Misconception: Students think escaping quote characters is equivalent to parameterization. Escaping is a denylist-style patch bypassable via encoding tricks or database-specific comment syntax.

content_blocks: SQL injection remains the canonical example of a trust-boundary failure: user input is concatenated directly into a command string that is then interpreted by a downstream engine as executable syntax rather than inert data. When username = request.form['username'] and password = request.form['password'] are concatenated into a raw SELECT statement, an attacker submitting admin' -- causes the resulting query to become SELECT id FROM users WHERE username = 'admin' -- ' AND password = '...', the trailing '--' comments out the password check entirely, bypassing authentication.

The defense is not 'better validation' of the input string, it is architectural: parameterized queries (also called prepared statements) separate the query's structure from its data at the protocol level, so no user-supplied value, regardless of what characters it contains, can ever be reinterpreted as SQL syntax.

slides.title: Parameterized Queries: Compile Structure First, Bind Data Second
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Parameterized queries are supported natively by virtually every modern database driver, this is a widely available, low-friction fix, not an exotic one.

Misconception: 'We use hash_password() so we're safe.' Hashing protects stored credentials at rest; it does nothing to prevent the query structure itself from being hijacked by concatenation.

Analogy: A mail-merge template where the recipient's name is inserted into a fixed letter, no matter what the recipient's name contains, it can never rewrite the letter's other paragraphs.

Exam tip: On free response, name BOTH the mechanism (structure compiled before data bound) and the outcome (values can never be reinterpreted as syntax) for full credit.
bullets: The mechanism: Query template with placeholders sent to the database separately from user-supplied values
Compile before bind: The database compiles the fixed query structure BEFORE any value is transmitted
Structural guarantee: Values are bound strictly as data, they can never alter the query's logical structure
Native driver support: PDO (PHP), java.sql.PreparedStatement (Java), parameterized cursor.execute() (Python DB-API)
Exam-critical distinction: 'Use parameterized queries' is the correct answer, not 'sanitize the input'

username = request.form['username']
password = request.form['password']

slides.title: Secure Defaults, Fail-Closed, and Least Privilege
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Least privilege is formalized in NIST SP 800-53 control AC-6, and this topic's study guide references it directly as enforcing permissions like chmod 700 owner-only restricts.

Misconception: Students think fail-open is more 'user-friendly' and therefore an acceptable trade-off. In security-critical paths (authentication, authorization), availability of the wrong kind is a liability, not a feature.

Analogy: An elevator that stops between floors during a power outage rather than continuing to move unpredictably, the safe failure mode is the one that limits harm.

Exam tip: When a scenario describes a system granting access after an authorization service times out, identify it as a fail-open design flaw and recommend fail-closed behavior.
bullets: Secure-by-default in practice: Unnecessary services disabled, default admin credentials removed, verbose errors suppressed in production
Least privilege: Grant only the minimum permissions required for a function, e.g., read-only where write isn't needed
Fail closed vs. fail open: Deny access when a control can't decide (expired session, unreachable auth service) rather than granting it by default
Why fail-closed wins: An ambiguous condition treated as 'deny' bounds the worst case; treated as 'allow' does not
Formalized by: NIST SP 800-53 control AC-6 (least privilege)

slides.speaker_notes:

content_blocks: Secure-by-default configuration means an application ships already hardened: unnecessary services disabled, default administrative credentials removed, verbose error messages suppressed in production, and permissions granted on a least-privilege basis by default rather than requiring an administrator to manually lock things down after installation. If a component only needs to read a table, it should not have write or delete permissions on that table.

A system that 'fails closed', denying access when a control cannot make a clear decision, such as an expired session or an unreachable authorization service, is markedly safer than one that 'fails open' and grants access by default under ambiguous conditions. Fail-closed bounds the worst-case outcome of an unexpected failure to 'legitimate access temporarily denied' rather than 'unauthorized access silently granted.'

slides.title: Content Security Policy: A Browser-Enforced Allowlist
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: The W3C Content Security Policy Level 3 specification is the governing standard. CSP is frequently paired with Subresource Integrity (SRI), which cryptographically verifies a third-party script hasn't been tampered with.

Misconception: Students think CSP replaces the need for output encoding. It is a compensating control, a second independent layer, not a substitute for the first.

Analogy: A guest list at a party's door, even if someone sneaks a note (script) inside through a crack in the window (encoding failure), the door guard (CSP) still checks whether anyone reading it aloud is on the approved list of speakers.

Exam tip: Know that CSP restricts WHICH ORIGINS may supply active content, while SRI verifies content from an approved origin hasn't been silently altered, these are two distinct, complementary controls.
bullets: CSP: An HTTP response header instructing the browser which sources of script/style/image content may load and execute
Defense in depth: Even if an XSS payload is reflected into the page, a strict CSP can prevent it from executing
default-src 'self': Fallback policy, only load content from the app's own origin unless overridden
script-src allowlist: An injected inline <script> or attacker-domain script is blocked outright by the browser
object-src 'none' / frame-ancestors 'none': Disables legacy plugins and prevents clickjacking via iframe embedding

content_blocks: One of the most effective secure-default browser controls available to web applications is the Content-Security-Policy header, which acts as a browser-enforced allowlist for where active content is permitted to load from. default-src 'self' is the fallback policy, only load content from the application's own origin unless overridden. script-src 'self' https://cdn.trusted-vendor.com means scripts may only execute if served from the app's own origin or one explicitly named vendor CDN, an attacker-injected inline script tag, or one pointing at an attacker-controlled domain, is blocked outright by the browser even if it made it into the page's HTML.

object-src 'none' disables legacy plugin content (Flash, Java applets), closing an old but still-relevant attack surface. frame-ancestors 'none' prevents the page from being embedded in an iframe on another site, mitigating clickjacking. CSP is a defense-in-depth layer, it does not replace output encoding, but substantially reduces the impact if encoding fails somewhere.

slides.title: Case Study: The 2017 Equifax Breach, an SDLC Response-Gate Failure
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: NIST SP 800-218's 'Respond to Vulnerabilities' practice group treats ongoing patch management as a first-class SDLC activity, not a separate IT operations concern.

Misconception: Students frame this purely as 'they had bad code.' The vulnerable code was in a third-party framework; the failure was organizational, not propagating a published patch into production for months.

content_blocks: In March 2017, the Apache Software Foundation disclosed CVE-2017-5638, a critical remote code execution flaw in the Apache Struts web framework, which Equifax used to power an online dispute portal. A patch was available within days, but Equifax's internal vulnerability management process failed to identify and patch the affected servers, and the flaw remained exploitable in production for over two months. Attackers exploited the unpatched instance beginning in mid-May 2017 and exfiltrated the personal data of approximately 147 million individuals.

From the perspective of Secure Web Application Design, Equifax illustrates a failure at the Response gate of the SDLC: a working patch existed, but the organization's asset inventory and patch management processes could not reliably identify which systems needed it. Investigations also identified an expired digital certificate that prevented intrusion-detection tooling from decrypting and inspecting traffic for over a year, and insufficient network segmentation that let attackers pivot from the dispute portal into unrelated sensitive databases. Equifax ultimately paid a global settlement exceeding $575 million.

slides.title: Case Study: The 2018 British Airways Magecart Attack, Missing CSP and SRI

quiz.question: Using the 2018 British Airways Magecart incident as a reference point, explain how a Content-Security-Policy header combined with Subresource Integrity would have functioned as defense-in-depth even if the attacker had already succeeded in modifying a first-party JavaScript file.
quiz.prompt: Address: (a) why TLS and PCI-DSS network controls provided no protection here; (b) what CSP's connect-src restriction would have blocked; (c) what SRI would have prevented independently of CSP.
quiz.explanation: Full-credit response: (a) The malicious script executed within the legitimate site's own trusted origin, so the compromise occurred entirely client-side, inside the victim's browser session, TLS protects data in transit and PCI-DSS network segmentation protects server-side infrastructure, neither of which is relevant once the trusted script itself has been altered. (b) A restrictive connect-src directive limits which network destinations the page may send data to; even though the tampered script originated from an allowed first-party path, CSP would have blocked the browser from transmitting captured card data to an unlisted, attacker-controlled exfiltration domain never present in the approved allowlist. (c) SRI addresses the initial tampering directly: had the script tag included an integrity attribute with the hash of the authentic file, the browser would have computed the hash of the actually-downloaded (tampered) script, detected the mismatch, and refused to execute it at all, independent of any CSP restriction on where data could later be sent. Together, SRI prevents execution of tampered code and CSP limits damage even if tampered code executes anyway, textbook defense-in-depth.

slides.title: Case Study: The 2018 British Airways Magecart Attack, Missing CSP and SRI

quiz.question: Using the 2018 British Airways Magecart incident as a reference point, explain how a Content-Security-Policy header combined with Subresource Integrity would have functioned as defense-in-depth even if the attacker had already succeeded in modifying a first-party JavaScript file.
quiz.prompt: Address: (a) why TLS and PCI-DSS network controls provided no protection here; (b) what CSP's connect-src restriction would have blocked; (c) what SRI would have prevented independently of CSP.
quiz.explanation: Full-credit response: (a) The malicious script executed within the legitimate site's own trusted origin, so the compromise occurred entirely client-side, inside the victim's browser session, TLS protects data in transit and PCI-DSS network segmentation protects server-side infrastructure, neither of which is relevant once the trusted script itself has been altered. (b) A restrictive connect-src directive limits which network destinations the page may send data to; even though the tampered script originated from an allowed first-party path, CSP would have blocked the browser from transmitting captured card data to an unlisted, attacker-controlled exfiltration domain never present in the approved allowlist. (c) SRI addresses the initial tampering directly: had the script tag included an integrity attribute with the hash of the authentic file, the browser would have computed the hash of the actually-downloaded (tampered) script, detected the mismatch, and refused to execute it at all, independent of any CSP restriction on where data could later be sent. Together, SRI prevents execution of tampered code and CSP limits damage even if tampered code executes anyway, textbook defense-in-depth.

slides.speaker_notes:
Context: The GDPR fine was later reduced from an initial proposed £183 million, partly due to COVID-19's economic impact on the airline industry.

Misconception: Students assume 'the server' is the only place trust boundaries need defending. A script running inside the customer's own browser, on the airline's own domain, is still crossing a trust boundary, between code the organization wrote/reviewed and code an attacker silently modified.

Analogy: A tampered vending machine inside a trusted building, customers trust the building, but someone altered what's actually dispensed once they're inside.

Exam tip: Be ready to explain how CSP and SRI address two DIFFERENT failure modes: CSP restricts where data can be SENT (exfiltration destination); SRI verifies content hasn't been TAMPERED WITH (integrity of the source).
content_blocks: In August–September 2018, attackers affiliated with Magecart, a web-skimming threat cluster, compromised the British Airways website by modifying a JavaScript file loaded by the payment page. The injected script, only 22 lines, silently captured customer name, address, and full payment card details (including CVV) as they were typed into the legitimate checkout form, transmitting that data in real time to an attacker-controlled server. Because the skimming script executed within the trusted context of the airline's own domain, standard payment-security controls like TLS and PCI-DSS network segmentation provided no protection, the theft happened entirely client-side, before the card data ever reached British Airways' servers.

Approximately 380,000 customer payment transactions were affected. The UK Information Commissioner's Office fined British Airways £20 million under GDPR, citing inadequate security testing and insufficient controls over third-party scripts on the payment page. A properly scoped script-src CSP directive would have prevented the browser from executing a script injected from, or exfiltrating data to, a domain not on the airline's explicit allowlist. SRI hashing on every first-party script would have caused the browser to reject the tampered file the instant its content diverged from the expected hash.

slides.title: DevSecOps: Shifting Security Left as a Positive Counter-Example
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: SCA tools (e.g., Snyk, Dependabot) specifically address the Equifax failure mode, an unpatched third-party dependency, by flagging known-vulnerable library versions automatically on every build.

Misconception: Students think DevSecOps just means 'run a scanner once before launch.' The defining feature is continuous, automated scanning integrated into every commit, not a one-time gate.

Analogy: A spell-checker that runs as you type rather than one you run once before printing the final document, catching mistakes the moment they're introduced is cheaper than catching them at the end.

Exam tip: If asked how an organization could have caught a vulnerability class 'before it reached production,' name shift-left/DevSecOps practices specifically: CI/CD-integrated SAST + SCA + mandatory peer review.
bullets: Shift-left philosophy: Embed SAST scanning directly into CI/CD pipelines rather than testing only before release
Peer review gate: Require review of every pull request against a secure coding checklist
Software Composition Analysis (SCA): Automated dependency-vulnerability scanning on every build
Measured outcome: Dramatically shorter mean time-to-remediate for newly discovered flaws
Direct connection: This exact pipeline would have flagged the profile.php reflection finding before it reached production

slides.title: Hardening Layer 1: Server-Side Input Enforcement
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Attackers routinely bypass browser-based validation entirely by crafting raw requests, this is documented directly in the study materials for this topic as a recurring misconception.

Misconception: 'We have client-side validation, so we're covered.' Client-side checks are a UX convenience only; they provide zero security guarantee.

Analogy: A 'no shoplifting' sign in a store window versus an actual security tag on the merchandise, the sign relies on voluntary compliance; the tag enforces the rule regardless of intent.

Exam tip: If a scenario mentions ONLY client-side (JavaScript form) validation as the security control, immediately flag it as insufficient and require server-side re-validation.
bullets: Rule: All validation logic must execute on the server, regardless of client-side checks for UX
Why: Browser-based JavaScript validation is trivially bypassed by direct API calls (curl, Burp Suite)
Default posture: Validation should default to allowlisting known-good formats
Ordering rule: All decoding/canonicalization must occur before validation logic runs
Never sufficient alone: Validation must be paired with output encoding and parameterized queries as independent layers

content_blocks: Organizations formalize secure web application design through layered technical, procedural, and organizational controls. Validation should default to allowlisting known-good formats, and all decoding/canonicalization must occur before validation logic runs, closing the canonicalization bypass class covered earlier. A recurring misconception is that a single well-written server-side filter is sufficient; it is not, even correct server-side input validation must be paired with output encoding and parameterized queries as independent, redundant layers, because input validation alone cannot anticipate every downstream context a piece of data will be used in.

slides.title: Hardening Layer 2: Output Encoding by Default in Frameworks
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: This principle generalizes beyond XSS, secure-by-default frameworks push the safe path to be the path of least resistance.

Misconception: Students think 'using React' automatically means an app is immune to XSS. It reduces the risk substantially, but any use of dangerouslySetInnerHTML (or equivalent) reintroduces the original vulnerability class.

Analogy: A car that requires the driver to explicitly and deliberately disable the seatbelt warning chime rather than one that ships with it off by default.

Exam tip: If a scenario mentions a framework-specific escape hatch (dangerouslySetInnerHTML, Django's |safe filter, Angular's bypassSecurityTrustHtml), recognize it as a deliberate reintroduction of the XSS risk that requires extra scrutiny.
bullets: Modern default: React, Angular, and Django templates apply HTML-context encoding automatically
Secure-by-default in action: Developers must actively opt out to reintroduce risk
Named escape hatches: React's dangerouslySetInnerHTML makes the unsafe path visibly deliberate
Why this matters: The unsafe path becomes an easy accidental default only when a developer bypasses it
Design lesson: Naming the dangerous function loudly is itself a security control

slides.speaker_notes:

content_blocks: Every point where untrusted data is written into a response, HTML body, HTML attribute, JavaScript context, URL, or CSS, must apply the encoding function specific to that context. Modern web frameworks apply HTML-context encoding automatically by default, which is itself an application of the secure-by-default principle; developers must actively opt out (e.g., React's dangerouslySetInnerHTML) to reintroduce risk, making the unsafe path visibly deliberate rather than an easy accidental default.

This is a direct illustration of how framework design choices operationalize secure-by-design at scale: rather than relying on every individual developer to remember to encode output correctly every time, the framework encodes by default and requires an explicit, loudly-named opt-out to disable that protection.

slides.title: Hardening Layer 3: Parameterization as an Enforced Standard
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: This mirrors how SAST tools are configured in practice, pattern-based rules (e.g., Semgrep, CodeQL queries) flag string-concatenation-into-execute() regardless of apparent exploitability.

Misconception: 'This concatenation is safe because the input isn't user-controlled right now.' Codebases change; a rule enforced categorically doesn't need to be re-litigated every time a new code path is added.

Analogy: A building code that bans a wiring pattern outright, rather than allowing it case-by-case wherever an electrician judges it 'probably fine', consistency prevents drift.

Exam tip: If asked why an organization would flag a concatenated query even when the immediate input source seems safe, cite defensive-by-default enforcement against future code changes, not just present-day exploitability.
bullets: Organizational enforcement: Code review gates and SAST rules flag any direct string concatenation into a database execute() call
Key nuance: The pattern itself is treated as the defect, regardless of whether the specific input appears attacker-controlled
Why 'appears safe' isn't good enough: Input sources change over time; a pattern that's safe today may not be tomorrow
The standard: Parameterized queries as a non-negotiable architectural requirement, not a per-case judgment call
Consequence: This shifts SQLi prevention from individual developer vigilance to systemic, automated enforcement

slides.title: Hardening Layer 4: Configuration Baselines and HSTS
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: HSTS is defined in RFC 6797. Configuration baselines like CIS Benchmarks provide vendor-agnostic, auditable hardening checklists across operating systems and platforms.

Misconception: Students think 'we redirect HTTP to HTTPS on the server' is equivalent to HSTS. A server-side redirect still requires one initial unencrypted request, which HSTS (once cached by the browser) eliminates entirely for subsequent visits.

Analogy: A standing instruction in your phone's contacts to only ever call someone on a secure line, even if you fumble and dial the insecure number, your phone auto-corrects to the secure route.

Exam tip: Know that HSTS is a browser-enforced, header-driven control distinct from a one-time server redirect, the distinction matters for downgrade-attack resistance.
bullets: Baseline provisioning: Systems provisioned from a hardened configuration baseline (e.g., CIS Benchmarks)
Baseline actions: Disables unused services, removes default credentials, enforces least-privilege permissions
Fail-closed default: Systems fail closed on ambiguous authorization decisions
HSTS: HTTP Strict Transport Security forces browsers to only ever connect over HTTPS, even if a link is typed as http://
Applies to: Any application handling authentication or sensitive data should enable HSTS by default

This topic's study guide decision framework states the pattern directly: 'If external public networks sniff client session headers → Enforce HTTPS HSTS and VPN tunnels', HSTS is the browser-side enforcement mechanism that makes 'always HTTPS' a guarantee rather than a hope dependent on every link being typed correctly.

slides.title: Compliance-Driven Verification: ASVS and SAMM
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: ASVS v4.0.3 and SAMM v2 are the current major versions referenced in the bibliography.

Misconception: Students conflate ASVS and SAMM as interchangeable compliance checklists. They operate at different scopes, one application (ASVS) versus one organization's whole program (SAMM).

Analogy: ASVS is a health inspection checklist for one restaurant; SAMM is an evaluation of the restaurant chain's overall food-safety management culture and training program.

Exam tip: If a scenario describes auditing a single application's security requirements, that's ASVS; if it describes assessing an organization's security program maturity across governance/design/verification, that's SAMM.
bullets: OWASP ASVS: A structured checklist of security requirements/verification tests across three levels of rigor
ASVS categories: 14 categories including V5 (Validation, Sanitization, Encoding) and V9 (Communications)
OWASP SAMM: Assesses the MATURITY of an organization's overall software security program
Key distinction: ASVS audits a specific application; SAMM assesses organizational program maturity
Purpose: Give organizations a structured way to measure and mature SDLC practices over time, not a one-time certification

The key distinction is scope: ASVS audits one application against a checklist; SAMM assesses whether the organization's processes that produce all its applications are maturing over time.

slides.title: The Layered Answer: Architectural, Procedural, Runtime

quiz.question: A free-response question asks how to prevent SQL injection in a described application. Which answer would earn full credit under the 'layered answer' rubric?
options: Sanitize all user input by escaping single quotes before building the query
Use parameterized queries only, with no mention of testing or runtime controls

Use parameterized queries (architectural), enforce SAST rules flagging string-concatenated queries in code review (procedural), and deploy a WAF with SQLi detection rules as a runtime backstop (runtime)
Install a web application firewall and rely on it exclusively to detect and block injection attempts
quiz.explanation: Option C is correct: it names one control at each of the three required layers -- architectural (parameterized queries), procedural (SAST/code review gate), and runtime (WAF backstop) -- matching the full-credit rubric. Option A is a weak, single-layer denylist-style answer. Option B is architecturally correct but single-layer, missing procedural and runtime controls. Option D relies solely on a runtime control and ignores the architectural fix entirely, which does not eliminate the vulnerability class.

slides.speaker_notes:
Context: This synthesizes Section II's technical controls (architectural), Section II's SDLC gates (procedural), and Section II's CSP discussion (runtime) into one exam-ready framework.

Misconception: Students name one correct control and stop, assuming that's sufficient for full credit. Full credit requires naming a control at each of the three layers.

Analogy: A bank vault: the vault door itself (architectural), the guard checking credentials at every shift (procedural), and the alarm system that triggers if someone still gets past both (runtime).

Exam tip: Memorize this three-layer template and practice applying it to SQLi, XSS, and misconfiguration scenarios, it is the single highest-leverage exam framework in this topic.

Layer 3, Runtime: CSP, WAF, and secure default configuration that reduce impact if the first two layers fail

slides.title: Detection Signals for Application-Layer Attacks
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: This directly complements Section II's mitigation/detection distinction and Section III's case studies, both of which involved detection gaps (Equifax's expired inspection certificate; the two-week undetected British Airways compromise).

Misconception: Students think a strong preventive control means detection is unnecessary. Detection provides the confirmation and early-warning layer that catches novel or unanticipated attack variants prevention wasn't designed for.

Analogy: A home security system with both locks (prevention) and cameras (detection), the locks stop most break-in attempts, but the cameras tell you if and when something got past them.

Exam tip: If asked to distinguish a mitigation from a detection control in a scenario, ask whether the control blocks the action (mitigation) or observes/alerts on it after the fact (detection).

Patch-gap detection: Asset inventory drift, servers running known-vulnerable framework versions
CSP reporting: The report-uri/report-to directive sends violation reports even in enforcement mode
Detection complements prevention: Prevention blocks the exploit; detection catches what prevention missed

Exam tip: If asked to distinguish a mitigation from a detection control in a scenario, ask whether the control blocks the action (mitigation) or observes/alerts on it after the fact (detection).
content_blocks: Beyond the architectural, procedural, and runtime prevention controls covered so far, mature security programs also instrument detection: a malformed SQL injection attempt that fails to balance quotes correctly often throws a parser exception, logged as a syntax error a SOC analyst can review. Similarly, a properly configured CSP can be deployed with a report-uri or report-to directive that sends violation reports to a monitoring endpoint even while the policy is actively enforcing (blocking) violations, giving defenders visibility into attempted XSS exploitation even when the browser successfully blocked it.

Asset inventory tooling that continuously tracks framework and library versions in production directly addresses the Equifax failure mode: detecting patch-gap drift (a server still running a known-vulnerable version after a patch has been published) before an attacker finds it. Detection does not replace prevention, it catches what prevention missed or provides confirmation that prevention is working as intended.

slides.title: Practice: Diagnose the Missing Control

quiz.question: For Scenario D (a tampered first-party script exfiltrated customer data to an attacker-controlled domain, mirroring the British Airways incident), name the two independent runtime controls that would have addressed this and explain what each one specifically prevents.
quiz.prompt: Name both controls and explain the distinct failure mode each one addresses.
quiz.explanation: Full-credit response: (1) A scoped Content-Security-Policy connect-src directive restricts which network destinations the page is permitted to send data to; even if the tampered script executed, the browser would refuse to transmit captured data to an attacker-controlled domain not present in the approved allowlist -- this addresses the EXFILTRATION step. (2) Subresource Integrity (SRI), applied via an integrity attribute containing the cryptographic hash of the authentic script, causes the browser to detect that the downloaded file no longer matches the expected hash and refuse to execute it at all -- this addresses the INITIAL TAMPERING/EXECUTION step, independent of CSP. Together they form defense-in-depth: SRI stops the malicious code from running in the first place; CSP limits the damage even if it somehow runs anyway.

slides.speaker_notes:
Context: This mirrors the cyber kill chain concept used elsewhere in the course, applied specifically to the application layer rather than network intrusion.

Stage 2, Weaponization: Craft a payload matched to the discovered gap (SQLi string, XSS script, RCE header)
Stage 3, Delivery/Exploitation: Submit the payload through the unmediated trust-boundary crossing
Stage 4, Execution: Data becomes code, the database runs it, the browser executes it, the OS runs it
Stage 5, Impact: Auth bypass, session hijack, data exfiltration, full compromise (Equifax, British Airways)

content_blocks: Every vulnerability class in this topic follows the same five-stage kill chain. Reconnaissance: the attacker identifies where the application reflects input unsafely, which framework version is running, or which security headers (CSP, HSTS) are absent, exactly the reconnaissance that preceded the Equifax and British Airways compromises. Weaponization: the attacker crafts a payload matched to the specific gap found, a SQL tautology, an XSS script tag, or a crafted header exploiting a known CVE.

Delivery/Exploitation: the payload crosses a trust boundary that lacked adequate mediation, unvalidated input, unencoded output, an unpatched framework. Execution: the fundamental failure at the heart of this entire topic occurs, data becomes code, whether interpreted by a database engine, a victim's browser, or an operating system shell. Impact: the consequence materializes, authentication bypass, session hijacking, mass data exfiltration, or full remote code execution, exactly as seen in every case study this topic examined.

Every control covered in this deck, SDLC gates, allowlisting, canonicalization ordering, parameterization, context-aware encoding, CSP, SRI, patch management, exists to break this chain at a specific stage, and the earlier in the chain a control intervenes, the less damage the attack can ultimately cause.

content_blocks: Before moving on, confirm fluency across five checkpoints. First, the SDLC gate order (Requirements, Design/Threat Modeling, Implementation, Verification, Release, Response) and which security activity belongs to each, a frequent exam trap tests whether you place SAST in Verification (correct) versus Implementation (incorrect).

Second, the allowlist-over-denylist argument and the canonicalization ordering rule (decode fully, then validate). Third, the specific remediation for each major vulnerability class: parameterized queries for SQL injection, context-aware output encoding for XSS, never 'just sanitize' as a standalone answer. Fourth, the precise distinction between CSP (restricts which origins may supply/receive content) and SRI (verifies content hasn't been tampered with), illustrated concretely by the British Airways case. Fifth, and most heavily tested: always answer prevention questions in three layers, architectural, procedural, and runtime, as modeled by the layered-answer framework.

big_idea.text: Input validation is a bouncer who checks every ID at the door of a form field. The safest version trusts nothing it hasn't verified itself, rather than trying to memorize every possible fake ID a guest might try to sneak past.
